title: Automated search for highly contextual Kochen-Specker proofs
abstract: Observable-based Kochen-Specker proofs are configurations of multi-qubit Pauli observables grouped into contexts whose products are plus or minus the indentity. Their robustness as state-independent contextuality tests can be measured by the tolerated error per context $\varepsilon = 2d/|H|$, where $d$ is the contextuality degree and $|H|$ the number of contexts. Since the degree depends only on an underlying abstract structure called the hypergram i.e. the pair formed by the context hypergraph and the anticommutation graph, the search for highly contextual proofs can be carried out on them instead, with no reference to qubits or to any particular Pauli labeling. We further exploit this by enumerating anticommutation graphs first, and then by associating to each graph $G$ the single hypergram carrying its entire hypergraph support $HS(G)$, so that exactly one candidate is examined per graph. Applied to the House of Graphs database and to censuses of vertex-transitive graphs on at most 24 vertices, this pipeline recovers the Peres-Mermin square, the doily and the Mermin pentagram, and yields configurations reaching $\varepsilon = 0.707$, against $0.424$ for the previous published record. The best configurations are predominantly those stemming from line graphs and unions of graphs; we explain the former by showing that every perfect matching of a graph is a context of its line graph, which exhibits the Peres-Mermin square and the doily as the first members of two infinite families. We close with finite geometric descriptions of the most striking configurations inside symplectic polar spaces, in terms of ovoids, hyperbolic quadrics and Fano planes.
summary: This paper presents a novel, graph-theoretic methodology to systematically search for the most contextually demanding quantum proofs (Kochen-Specker type). By abstracting the problem to the 'hypergram' structure, the authors achieved record-high contextuality measures ($\varepsilon=0.707$) by analyzing graph structures, providing deep insights into the mathematical limits of quantum contextuality.
main_problem: The paper aims to automate the search for highly contextual Kochen-Specker proofs, which test the fundamental assumption of quantum mechanics that measurement outcomes are independent of the measurement context.
main_result: The authors developed a graph-theoretic pipeline that recovered known highly contextual proofs and achieved a record tolerated error per context ($\varepsilon$) of 0.707, primarily by analyzing disjoint unions of graphs.
method: The search is formalized by abstracting the problem to the 'hypergram' structure derived from an anticommutation graph, allowing the search to proceed independently of specific qubit labels.
model_or_system: The model involves multi-qubit Pauli observables and their associated contextuality structure, formalized using hypergraphs and anticommutation graphs. The analysis is deeply rooted in algebraic graph theory and linear algebra over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
key_observables: Contextuality Degree ($d$) and Tolerated Error per Context ($\varepsilon = 2d/|H|$).
important_parameters: The structure of the underlying graph $G$, the size of the graph (e.g., up to 24 vertices), and the number of contexts $|H|$.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that restricting the search to the hypergram formed by the full hypergraph support $	ext{HS}(G)$ of an anticommutation graph $G$ is sufficient to find the highest $\varepsilon$ values.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the construction process from a graph to its context hypergraph and associated quantum assignment, showing examples like the doily and Mermin pentagram within symplectic polar spaces.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the mathematical framework by defining the hypergram and the measure $\varepsilon$. It then details a systematic search strategy by enumerating anticommutation graphs and applying the $	ext{HS}(G)$ construction. Results are presented by recovering known proofs and establishing new records using graph families and geometric analogies.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, abstract, and systematic mathematical framework (graph theory) to probe fundamental non-classical features of quantum theory, which is highly relevant for understanding the limits of quantum computation and measurement theory.

Figure 3: A doily (middle) in W3 lying on a certain hyperbolic quadric, one of its spread of lines (five colored pairwise disjoint lines) and one of the two associated Mermin pentagrams. An edge of the pentagram of a given color forms with the line of the doily that is of the same color a Fano plane.

Figure 4: A portrayal of the fact that 25 observables of our L(K5,5)-configuration can be par- titioned into five pentads in two different ways; the five pentads in one set are represented by pentagons, the ones in the other set by lines. Each context thus picks up one observable from each pentad.

Figure 5: The composition of the Chang configuration. The central (Mermin) pentagram features ten points of order eight and the six concurrent Fano planes (the line of concurrence is always represented by a circle) comprise 18 observables of order ten (colored). Each observable of the pentagram is the meet of three colors and it commutes with each observable in the Fano planes of the corresponding colors.
